newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to mark 50th birthday with Islamic summit.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to mark 50th birthday with Islamic summit.

text.p: Pakistan will celebrate its 50th anniversary of independence by hosting an Islamic summit on Sunday at which ceremony seems likely to outweigh substance.
During its one-day meeting the 51-member Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC) will consider a vague one-point agenda on "preparing the Islamic world for the 21st century".
Foreign ministry officials say they expect 1,500 delegates and journalists to fly into Islamabad for what they said would be the OIC's first-ever extraordinary summit.
"It is to underline the solidarity of Islamic countries with Pakistan and Pakistan's solidarity with the Islamic world," summit spokesman Inamul Haq told a news briefing this week.

Islamic Pakistan, along with its arch-rival India, gained independence from British rule in 1947, when the sub-continent suffered the upheaval of partition and many thousands lost their lives in Hindu-Moslem violence.
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and Turkish President Suleyman Demirel are the most prominent heads of state due to attend what diplomats said could prove a low-key summit.
Crown Prince Abdullah of Saudi Arabia has promised to come, but few heavyweight Arab leaders are expected to show up.
Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, citing Middle East tension, is staying away, as are Syria's President Hafez al-Assad, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and King Hussein of Jordan.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, due to visit Sri Lanka next week, may turn up unless the crisis over Israel's decision to build a Jewish settlement in Arab east Jerusalem detains him.
But no heads of state from the Gulf or main North African countries are expected to attend, with the possible exception of Morocco's King Hassan, the OIC's current chairman.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina of Bangladesh, which seceded from Pakistan in 1971, will be one of the few women leaders at the event, which coincides with Pakistan's national day.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government, elected on February 3, has had to take over final preparations for what ousted premier Benazir Bhutto envisaged as a glittering affair when she persuaded the OIC in 1995 to hold the summit.

Meraj Khalid, who led a three-month caretaker administration after Bhutto's November 5 downfall, even suggested that the event should be scrapped because Pakistan had little to celebrate and could not afford a costly birthday party.
Nevertheless, feverish work has been under way for the past few weeks to complete a new convention centre where the summit will take place and prepare accommodation for the delegates.
Air force jets scream almost daily over the leafy city, nestled beneath the Margalla Hills, practising for a fly-past during the traditional March 23 military parade.
This year the OIC delegates will witness the parade down Islamabad's central avenue, named after the nation's founder Mohammad Ali Jinnah, before holding two summit sessions.

Thousands of army troops and paramilitary soldiers have moved into residential areas of the capital, setting up makeshift camps, some of which contain tents carrying the markings of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees.
